claim: The cerebral cortex and cerebellum both play important roles in sensorimotor processing.
source: The cerebral cortex and cerebellum both play important roles in sensorimotor processing, however, precise connections between these major brain structures remain elusive.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established scientific consensus about the roles of these brain structures.

claim: Precise connections between the cerebral cortex and cerebellum remain elusive.
source: The cerebral cortex and cerebellum both play important roles in sensorimotor processing, however, precise connections between these major brain structures remain elusive.
evidence: This statement reflects the motivation for the study and is supported by the need for the research presented.

claim: There is a highly organized topography of corticopontine projections in mice.
source: We confirm a highly organized topography of corticopontine projections in mice
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from anterograde tracing experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: There are no corticopontine projections originating from primary auditory cortex.
source: however, we found no corticopontine projections originating from primary auditory cortex
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations from AAV1.cre injections into A1 showing no labeled cells in pontine nuclei.

claim: Several potential extra-pontine cerebrocerebellar pathways exist.
source: we found no corticopontine projections originating from primary auditory cortex and detail several potential extra-pontine cerebrocerebellar pathways.
evidence: This is supported by data showing labeled cells in various brainstem nuclei outside the pontine nuclei.

claim: The cerebellar hemispheres were the major target of resulting disynaptic mossy fiber terminals.
source: The cerebellar hemispheres were the major target of resulting disynaptic mossy fiber terminals
evidence: This is supported by quantification of mossy fiber terminals showing the majority in cerebellar hemispheres.

claim: At least sparse cerebrocerebellar projections exist to every lobule of the cerebellum.
source: but we also found at least sparse cerebrocerebellar projections to every lobule of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data showing mossy fiber terminals in all cerebellar lobules.

claim: Projections originating from association cortex resulted in less laterality than primary sensory/motor cortices.
source: Notably, projections originating from association cortex resulted in less laterality than primary sensory/motor cortices.
evidence: This is supported by quantification showing different ratios of ipsilateral to contralateral projections for association versus primary cortices.

claim: Spatial overlap of mossy fiber terminals from functionally distinct cortical areas occurs within crus I, paraflocculus, and vermal regions IV/V and VI.
source: Within molecularly defined cerebellar modules we found spatial overlap of mossy fiber terminals, originating from functionally distinct cortical areas, within crus I, paraflocculus, and vermal regions IV/V and VI
evidence: This is supported by anatomical mapping data showing terminal locations from different cortical regions in these cerebellar areas.

claim: Crus I, paraflocculus, and vermal regions IV/V and VI are potential hubs for multimodal cortical influence.
source: highlighting these regions as potential hubs for multimodal cortical influence.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial overlap data showing convergence of multiple cortical inputs in these regions.

claim: The environment provides constantly updating sensory signals that must be acted upon for an animal to perform basic behaviors necessary for survival.
source: The environment provides constantly updating sensory signals that must be acted upon for an animal to perform basic behaviors necessary for survival, including navigating through the environment, feeding/foraging, and other goal-directed behaviors.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about animal behavior and sensory processing.

claim: Perception and action loops require various sensory modalities to be integrated and translated into directed motor output.
source: These perception and action loops require various sensory modalities (i.e. somatosensation, audition, and vision) to be integrated and translated into directed motor output.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of sensorimotor integration.

claim: Both the cerebral cortex and the cerebellum are major brain regions involved in sensorimotor integration and translation.
source: Both the cerebral cortex (Stein and Stanford, 2008) and the cerebellum (Snider and Stowell, 1944; Rondi-Reig et al., 2014; Baumann et al., 2015) are major brain regions involved in this sensorimotor integration and translation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Connections between the cerebral cortex and cerebellum form one of the largest projection pathways in the brain.
source: Connections between these two brain regions form one of the largest projection pathways in the brain
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Selective expansion of the cortico-cerebellar system occurs across evolution.
source: selective expansion of this cortico-cerebellar system occurs across evolution (Gutiérrez-Ibáñez et al., 2018; Smaers and Vanier, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to evolutionary studies.

claim: The precise functions of cerebrocerebellar pathways are not fully understood.
source: This reflects the importance of cerebrocerebellar communication, however, the precise functions of these pathways are not fully understood (Apps and Watson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: It has been difficult to study the organization of cerebrocerebellar connections in precise detail due to their indirect nature.
source: Due to the indirect nature of cerebrocerebellar connections, it has been difficult to study their organization in precise detail.
evidence: This is based on methodological limitations in the field.

claim: A large body of research has mapped out corticopontine projections.
source: While a large body of research has mapped out the corticopontine projections (Brodal and Bjaalie, 1997; Glickstein, 1997; Leergaard and Bjaalie, 2007; Proville et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: A large body of research has mapped out pontocerebellar projections.
source: or the pontocerebellar projections (Pijpers and Ruigrok, 2006; Pakan et al., 2010; Proville et al., 2014; Biswas et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Few studies have utilized neurotropic viruses to study cerebrocerebellar pathways.
source: few studies have utilized neurotropic viruses (Kelly and Strick, 2003; Suzuki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing limited use of this methodology.

claim: The precise routes for information flow from the cortex to the cerebellum have remained largely inferred.
source: Therefore, the precise routes for information flow from the cortex to the cerebellum, including detailed terminal organization in the highly modular cerebellar cortex, have remained largely inferred.
evidence: This is inferred from the limitations of previous methodologies.

claim: The integration of multimodal inputs to the cerebellum is a fundamental operation that would allow for the precise coordination of sensory-driven movements.
source: The integration of multimodal inputs to the cerebellum is a fundamental operation that would allow for the precise coordination of sensory-driven movements within this brain region.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about cerebellar function.

claim: The potential for a single granule cell to receive multimodal input via both descending motor cortex and ascending proprioceptive pathways has been shown in mice.
source: Anatomically, the potential for a single granule cell to receive multimodal input via both descending motor cortex and ascending proprioceptive pathways has been shown in mice (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The potential for co-innervation originating from various cortical areas spanning multiple modalities is unknown, even on the regional level in the cerebellum.
source: However, the potential for co-innervation originating from various cortical areas spanning multiple modalities is unknown, even on the regional level in the cerebellum
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Co-innervation from various cortical areas has consequences for the role of cerebro-cerebellar-cerebro feedback loops in learning and predictive motor control.
source: and has consequences for the role of cerebro-cerebellar-cerebro feedback loops in learning and predictive motor control (e.g. Chabrol et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a theoretical implication.

claim: AAV1.cre acts as a mono-trans-synaptic anterograde tracer that crosses a single functional synapse.
source: we utilized an AAV1.cre construct that has been shown to act as a trans-synaptic anterograde tracer that crosses a single functional synapse (mono-trans-synaptic; Zingg et al., 2017; Zingg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: Injections into A1 produced only terminal labeling in the pons.
source: with the notable exception that injections into A1 produced only terminal labeling in the pons
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations from the study.

claim: There is a lack of an A1-ponto-cerebellar pathway in mice.
source: indicating the lack of a A1-ponto-cerebellar pathway in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of labeled pontine cells after A1 injections.

claim: The majority of labeled mossy fiber terminals from primary sensory and motor cortical regions were in the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere.
source: The majority of labeled mossy fiber terminals from the primary sensory and motor cortical regions were in the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere
evidence: This is supported by quantification of terminal locations.

claim: Cortical influences were not restricted to the cerebellar hemispheres, as terminals spanned all regions of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Cortical influences were not restricted to the cerebellar hemispheres, as terminals spanned all regions of the cerebellar cortex, with biases depending on the cortical modality.
evidence: This is supported by mapping data showing terminals throughout the cerebellum.

claim: Cerebellar subdivisions with the highest regional co-innervation of multimodal inputs were crus I, the paraflocculus, vermal lobule VI and lobules IV/V.
source: Cerebellar subdivisions with the highest regional co-innervation of multimodal inputs were crus I, the paraflocculus (PFl), vermal lobule VI and lobules IV/V
evidence: This is supported by quantification of terminal overlap from different cortical regions.

claim: Following cortical injections, mono-trans-synaptically labeled cells were found in the ipsilateral basal pontine nuclei from all cortical target regions, with the exception of A1.
source: Following cortical injections, mono-trans-synaptically labeled cells were found in the ipsilateral basal pontine nuclei (referred to as pontine nuclei throughout) from all cortical target regions, with the exception of A1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: After injections in the dorsal secondary auditory region AuD, a corticopontine pathway was observed.
source: In contrast, after injections in the more dorsal secondary auditory region, AuD, a corticopontine pathway was observed (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The lack of corticopontine projections from A1 was confirmed by injecting CAV.cre into the pontine nuclei.
source: The lack of corticopontine projections from A1, was confirmed by injecting CAV.cre into the pontine nuclei; this viral vector is preferentially taken up by axon terminals, resulting in retrograde labeling.
evidence: This is supported by retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: Retrogradely labeled cells were found in AuD and more ventral auditory cortex (AuV), but no labeled cells in A1.
source: Here we found retrogradely labeled cells in AuD and more ventral auditory cortex (AuV), but no labeled cells in A1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Labeled fibers were found in the dorsomedial portion of the ipsilateral pons following A1 injections.
source: Although anterogradely labeled cell bodies were not observed in the pontine nuclei following AAV1.cre injections in A1, labeled fibers were found in the dorsomedial portion of the ipsilateral pons (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Fibers observed in the pons after A1 injections could be traversing through the pons towards lower brainstem structures.
source: These fibers could be either traversing through the pons, potentially towards lower brainstem structures (e.g., cochlear and vestibular nuclei see Figure 2A; see also Budinger et al., 2000)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation and anatomical observations.

claim: Fibers observed in the pons after A1 injections could be disynaptic terminals resulting from labeled indirect pathways from A1 to the pontine nuclei, likely via the inferior colliculus.
source: or disynaptic terminals resulting from labeled indirect pathways from A1 to the pontine nuclei, likely via the inferior colliculus (Schuller et al., 1991b; Caicedo and Herbert, 1993).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Anterogradely labeled neurons were consistently observed in the inferior colliculus after A1 injections.
source: Indeed, anterogradely labeled neurons were consistently observed in the inferior colliculus after A1 injections (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Following injection of AAV1.cre in the inferior colliculus, anterogradely labeled cells were found in the pontine nuclei as well as mossy fiber terminals in the cerebellum.
source: and following injection of AAV1.cre in the inferior colliculus, anterogradely labeled cells were found in the pontine nuclei as well as mossy fiber terminals in the cerebellum, demonstrating the potential for a trisynaptic A1-collicular-cerebellar pathway via the pontine nuclei (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Resulting pontine labeling after cortical injections in mice was topographically organized with more rostral cortical regions projecting more medially in the pons and caudal cortical areas projecting towards the lateral extent of the pontine nuclei.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Leergaard and Bjaalie, 2007; for review see, Kratochwil et al., 2017), resulting pontine labeling after cortical injections in mice was topographically organized with more rostral cortical regions projecting more medially in the pons and caudal cortical areas projecting towards the lateral extent of the pontine nuclei (Figure 1E, see also Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Most pontine labeling was strictly ipsilateral.
source: While most pontine labeling was strictly ipsilateral
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: M1 was the only cortical target region that resulted in bilateral pontine labeling.
source: M1 was the only cortical target region that resulted in bilateral pontine labeling (average of 118 ± 36 neurons ipsilateral to 8 ± 3 neurons contralateral; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of labeled cells shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Previous anterograde tracer studies have observed corticopontine fibers largely in the ipsilateral pontine nuclei with relatively sparse labeling in the contralateral pons.
source: Previous anterograde tracer studies have observed corticopontine fibers largely in the ipsilateral pontine nuclei with relatively sparse labeling in the contralateral pons (Mihailoff et al., 1985; Leergaard and Bjaalie, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It was unclear if sparse contralateral corticopontine projections were fibers of passage or axon terminals.
source: However, it was unclear if these sparse contralateral projections were fibers of passage or axon terminals
evidence: This identifies a previous uncertainty in the field.

claim: Sparse contralateral corticopontine projections are axon terminals for M1 projections.
source: our results suggest the later for M1 projections and the former for all other cortical targets regions described here.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of labeled cells in contralateral pons after M1 injections.

claim: Sparse contralateral corticopontine projections are fibers of passage for all cortical target regions except M1.
source: our results suggest the later for M1 projections and the former for all other cortical targets regions described here.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of labeled cells in contralateral pons after non-M1 injections.

claim: The existence of functional synapses for contralateral corticopontine projections was also reported in primates, exclusively after M1 injections.
source: Interestingly, the existence of functional synapses for contralateral corticopontine projections was also reported in primates, however, also exclusively after M1 injections (Morecraft et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to research in primates.

claim: Anterogradely labeled cells were observed in various other precerebellar nuclei.
source: We observed anterogradely labeled cells in various other precerebellar nuclei (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1B; see also Ruigrok et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After S1 injections, more labeled cells were found in extra-pontine precerebellar nuclei than in pontine nuclei (70 ± 8% of total labeling).
source: In fact, after S1 injections we found more labeled cells in extra-pontine precerebellar nuclei than in pontine nuclei (70 ± 8% of total labeling)
evidence: This is supported by quantification of labeled cells.

claim: After M1 injections, just under half (40 ± 3%) of labeled cells were in extra-pontine precerebellar nuclei.
source: and after M1 injections, just under half (40 ± 3%).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of labeled cells.

claim: Labeled cells were observed in several precerebellar nuclei including the red nucleus, reticulotegmental nucleus, spinal trigeminal nucleus, lateral reticular nucleus, matrix region x, and vestibular nuclei.
source: This labeling spanned several precerebellar nuclei, including the red nucleus and reticulotegmental nucleus, as well as more caudal brainstem regions including the spinal trigeminal nucleus, lateral reticular nucleus, the matrix region x and the vestibular nuclei (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The reticulotegmental nucleus is classified as a separate extra-pontine region in this study.
source: While the reticulotegmental nucleus is often grouped together with the basal pontine nuclei, these regions in the pons appear to play different functional roles (Cicirata et al., 2005), hence, in this study we classify the reticulotegmental nucleus as a separate extra-pontine region.
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citation.

claim: Labeled fibers were observed in both the medial and inferior cerebellar peduncles.
source: Additionally, we observed labeled fibers in both the medial and inferior cerebellar peduncles (see Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Disynaptic tracts project to the cerebellum from pontine regions and more caudal extra-pontine precerebellar nuclei.
source: indicating disynaptic tracts projecting to the cerebellum from pontine regions and more caudal extra-pontine precerebellar nuclei, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of labeled fibers in cerebellar peduncles.

claim: Since there was no labeling observed in the pontine nuclei after A1 injections, the resulting mossy fiber terminals must reach the cerebellum through other precerebellar nuclei.
source: Since there was no labeling observed in the pontine nuclei after A1 injections, the resulting mossy fiber terminals must reach the cerebellum through other precerebellar nuclei, of which we found labeling in the vestibular as well as the cochlear nuclei (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the absence of pontine labeling but presence of cerebellar terminals.

claim: No labeled cells were observed from any target cortical region in the spinal or lateral vestibular nuclei, the external cuneate nucleus, or the inferior olive.
source: We did not observe labeled cells from any target cortical region in the spinal or lateral vestibular nuclei, the external cuneate nucleus, or the inferior olive.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Fibers and terminal labeling were observed in the inferior olive following injections in S1.
source: We did, however, observe fibers and terminal labeling in the inferior olive following injections in S1 (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fibers and terminal labeling were observed in the inferior olive to a lesser extent after injections in M1.
source: and to a lesser extent after injections in M1.

claim: Only after S1 and M1 injections, anterogradely labeled cells were observed in the matrix region x.
source: Interestingly, also only after S1 and M1 injections, anterogradely labeled cells were observed in the matrix region x, which has been suggested as a candidate preolivary relay nucleus (Ackerley et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citation.

claim: There is controversy regarding the existence of direct cerebro-olivary connections in rodents, particularly originating from M1.
source: There is some controversy regarding the existence of direct cerebro-olivary connections in rodents, particularly originating from M1 (Swenson et al., 1989; Baker et al., 2001; Ackerley et al., 2006); for review see Watson and Apps, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The results support disynaptic input from the cerebral cortex to inferior olivary neurons.
source: our results support disynaptic input from the cerebral cortex to inferior olivary neurons.

claim: Sparse fibers were observed in the lateral cerebellar nucleus following S1 and M1 injections, likely from pontocerebellar collaterals.
source: Sparse fibers were also observed in the lateral cerebellar nucleus following S1 and M1 injections, likely from pontocerebellar collaterals (Cicirata et al., 2005; Biswas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations.

claim: Cerebrocerebellar mossy fiber terminal labeling in the granule cell layer of the cerebellum was systematically present, regardless of the cortical origin.
source: Cerebrocerebellar mossy fiber terminal labeling in the granule cell layer of the cerebellum was systematically present, regardless of the cortical origin (e.g. Figure 1F, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1F.

source: We did not find AAV1.cre-induced tdTomato expressing granule cells or Purkinje cells in any of the cases

claim: The AAV construct did not transfer to higher-order downstream structures beyond mono-synaptic connections.
source: indicating that the AAV construct did not transfer to higher-order downstream structures beyond mono-synaptic connections (see also Zingg et al., 2017; Zingg et al., 2020).

source: Cerebrocerebellar projections were largely, but not exclusively, to the contralateral cerebellum (average across all animals: contralateral 70 ± 3%, ipsilateral 30 ± 3%).
